title: Technical deep dive: cache hit-rate + cost (Aurora)
next_steps: Redwood to share cache telemetry one-pager (metric definitions + labels + cardinality policy) and sample dashboard screenshots.
Aurora to send a 24h request-shape summary (prompt token histogram, % streaming chat, target regions) for Redwood to estimate cache upside and expected hit-rate bands.
Schedule a follow-up in 1 week to review a proposed Dedicated topology (region(s), routing locality knobs) and a draft pilot success plan focused on $/resolved ticket.
action_items: Owner: Allison Grant — Send Aurora the current cache dashboard panel list (hit-rate, miss reasons, eviction pressure, wasted prefill) and alerting guardrails by 2025-03-20
Owner: Omar El-Sayed — Provide metric definitions for prefix cache vs KV cache (including partial-hit and streaming retry semantics) and recommended sampling defaults by 2025-03-20
Owner: Miguel Santos — Share pilot proposal template + security data handling note (no raw prompts; hashed/bucketed features) by 2025-03-21
Owner: Karen Liu — Confirm Aurora’s preferred deployment mode (Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private VPC) and required regions by 2025-03-22
Owner: Devon Marshall — Send 3 representative conversation templates and whether prompts can be canonicalized (system + tools + separators) by 2025-03-22
topics: Cost drivers: prefill vs decode, long system prompts, multi-turn chat repetition
Prefix cache hit-rate vs KV cache reuse effectiveness (what’s measured and what it means)
Routing locality: region pinning, model version pinning, and avoiding cross-pool cache misses
Miss reason taxonomy (capacity/eviction, TTL expired, policy disabled, hash mismatch, version mismatch)
Telemetry surfaces: dashboards, alerts, and a first-pass recommendation report
Privacy + cardinality controls: avoiding per-tenant explosions, bucketing prompt lengths
questions: Can Redwood attribute cache misses to version mismatch vs hash mismatch (prompt differences) reliably?
Will streaming retries double-count cache misses/hits in the metrics?
Can we slice hit-rate by route/model/region without metric cardinality going crazy?
What knobs can Aurora control (TTL, max cache bytes, per-route caching, routing policy) and what are safe defaults?
summary: Aurora is evaluating Redwood primarily to reduce inference cost for a support-agent/chat workload with long system prompts and high repetition across turns. The team asked for concrete cache telemetry: prefix cache hit-rate, KV reuse depth/effectiveness, eviction/pressure indicators, and "wasted prefill" to quantify when prefill work doesn’t translate into reuse. Redwood clarified definitions (including partial hits), explained how locality (region/model-version routing) impacts hit-rate, and outlined how telemetry is exposed (dashboards + guarded labels + sampling). Aurora’s main concerns were (1) differentiating real hit-rate changes vs telemetry gaps, (2) ensuring metrics aren’t inflated by streaming retries, and (3) getting actionable levers for operators rather than just graphs.
transcript:
Fireflies.ai Transcript

Meeting: Technical deep dive: cache hit-rate + cost (Aurora)
Date: 2025-03-18
Time: 19:00 UTC
Duration: 52 min
Attendees:
- Miguel Santos (Redwood) — Customer Success
- Omar El-Sayed (Redwood) — Staff, Runtime
- Allison Grant (Redwood) — Senior Observability Engineer
- Karen Liu (Aurora) — VP Engineering
- Devon Marshall (Aurora) — Staff ML Engineer
- Priya Desai (Aurora) — Infra/SRE
- Ben Torres (Aurora) — Procurement

---

[00:00] Miguel Santos: Cool. I think we’re all on. Thanks everyone. Goal today is, um, go deeper than the demo did on cache hit-rate and what telemetry we can actually give you so you can drive cost down. Omar is here from runtime, Allison from observability.

[00:17] Karen Liu: Great, thanks. Yeah, we’re pretty focused on unit economics. Like dollars per resolved ticket. We think cache is the big lever because our system prompt is… massive.

[00:28] Devon Marshall: It’s like 2k to 4k tokens just for the policy and tools list, depending on tenant.

[00:35] Omar El-Sayed: Yep, that’s exactly where prefix caching helps. Maybe we start with what you mean by “cache” today. Are you doing any prompt memoization on your side?

[00:45] Devon Marshall: We do a little. We cache final answers for some FAQ-ish flows, but for the agent chat it’s not reliable. We don’t really cache model internals obviously.

[00:55] Priya Desai: And we’re on Azure OpenAI right now. We can’t see much besides tokens in/out and latency. When it spikes, we’re guessing.

[01:07] Miguel Santos: Yep, that’s consistent. So Redwood has two relevant caches in the runtime. One is prefix cache — basically reuse of the prefill computation when the beginning of prompts repeat. The other is KV cache reuse inside a conversation / across turns depending on routing and policy.

[01:25] Karen Liu: When you say “KV cache across turns,” do you mean persistent across requests? Or within a single request?

[01:33] Omar El-Sayed: Across requests, but only when we can guarantee it’s safe and the routing keeps you on the same cache locality. Think: repeated chat turns where the first N tokens are identical. We store the computed attention keys/values for those tokens. Next turn we can skip recomputing that segment.

[01:52] Devon Marshall: So it’s like caching the transformer state for those tokens.

[01:55] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. But it’s sensitive to prompt canonicalization. Like if a timestamp changes, or whitespace, or tool list ordering, that breaks the hash.

[02:06] Priya Desai: That’s what we worry about. Our system message includes like request IDs and some tracing IDs.

[02:12] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah, that would crush hit-rate. One thing we do in recommendations is basically flag “hash mismatch misses” and suggest canonicalization. But I want to be clear what the telemetry can tell you.

[02:25] Allison Grant: From the observability side, we’ll show hit-rate as a metric with strict labels. We don’t store prompts. We store bucketed features like prompt-length bins, and we can attribute misses to reason codes.

[02:40] Karen Liu: Can you define hit-rate precisely? Because we’ve seen vendors claim a 70% hit-rate but it’s like, meaningless.

[02:47] Omar El-Sayed: Totally. So for prefix cache hit-rate: we define it as reused prefill tokens divided by eligible prefill tokens. Eligible means tokens in the prefill phase that could have been reused given caching is enabled for the route and the prompt is long enough.

[03:04] Devon Marshall: What about partial hits? Like first 1500 tokens match, then diverge.

[03:08] Omar El-Sayed: That’s a hit for those 1500 tokens. Telemetry includes a histogram for “reuse depth” — how many tokens were reused per request, bucketed. So you can see if you’re mostly getting shallow reuse or deep reuse.

[03:23] Karen Liu: And KV cache reuse… is that the same metric?

[03:27] Omar El-Sayed: Related but slightly different. Prefix cache is about skipping prefill compute for a prefix. KV reuse effectiveness includes, like, did the cached KV actually get used through decode. The reason we separate it is because you can have “wasted prefill.”

[03:43] Priya Desai: Wasted prefill meaning you did work and then didn’t get benefit?

[03:47] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. Example: you do a big prefill, but due to eviction pressure, the cache entry is gone by the time the next request could reuse it. Or you routed to a different region/pool. So we track “wasted prefill tokens” as a counter — tokens computed in prefill that did not contribute to subsequent reuse. It’s not perfect, but it’s a strong signal when cache is thrashing.

[04:10] Devon Marshall: That would be huge. Because right now all we see is prefill tokens and latency, and we just argue about whether it’s “model slower” or “traffic different.”

[04:20] Allison Grant: Right, and we also emit eviction counts and a pressure gauge. Pressure is like how close the cache is to configured max bytes / how aggressive eviction is. So if hit-rate drops and pressure spikes, it’s a capacity thing.

[04:35] Karen Liu: What about distinguishing capacity vs TTL expiry?

[04:39] Omar El-Sayed: We categorize misses into a stable taxonomy: capacity/evicted, TTL expired, policy disabled, hash mismatch, version mismatch. Version mismatch is big during model rollouts.

[04:55] Karen Liu: Wait, version mismatch miss means you changed the model and now cache is invalid.

[04:59] Omar El-Sayed: Yeah. Or even same model family but different weights version. Cache key includes model version for safety.

[05:08] Priya Desai: That’s one of our pain points. We do gradual rollouts and it changes throughput. We can’t tell if the cost jump is due to cache invalidation.

[05:16] Allison Grant: In the dashboards, you can filter by model version and see hit-rate segmented. We also recommend pinning versions per route during rollouts if cache benefit is important, or using canary with clear expectations that hit-rate will dip.

[05:32] Ben Torres: Sorry, can I ask a… business question? Is this telemetry available in Hosted, or only Dedicated?

[05:38] Miguel Santos: It’s available across Hosted and Dedicated. For Private, it depends on deployment package, but yes—same metrics. For Hosted we apply stricter sampling and label guardrails to keep cost sane.

[05:52] Ben Torres: Sampling meaning you’re not collecting every request?

[05:56] Allison Grant: Correct. Especially for high volume routes. But we sample in a way that keeps hit-rate statistically stable, and we always keep the aggregate counters consistent. Some of the higher-cardinality debug signals go to traces with sampling.

[06:12] Devon Marshall: Okay, about slicing. We need to be able to slice by tenant. Otherwise it’s not actionable for us.

[06:18] Allison Grant: We generally don’t allow raw tenant_id as a metric label in Hosted because it explodes series count. What we do: (1) route-level slicing is always available, and route often maps to tenant in your gateway design; (2) for Dedicated and Private you can opt into more granular slicing because it’s your infra budget; (3) we can provide a “top-N tenants by traffic” view via an offline aggregate table rather than high-cardinality metrics.

[06:46] Karen Liu: Offline aggregate table is fine. We just need chargeback and to find the worst offenders.

[06:52] Miguel Santos: That aligns with the recommendations MVP we discussed. It’s basically a batch job that outputs, per route (and optionally per top tenant), what’s happening and what to change.

[07:05] Devon Marshall: What kind of recommendations? Like “turn on caching?”

[07:08] Omar El-Sayed: More specific. Example: “Your prompt-length bucket 2k-4k has low reuse depth and high hash-mismatch misses. Suggest canonicalizing system prompt: remove request_id/timestamp fields from the cached prefix.” Or “High eviction pressure + high wasted prefill: increase max_prefix_cache_bytes or adjust TTL.”

[07:33] Priya Desai: Can we control those knobs per route?

[07:36] Omar El-Sayed: In Dedicated and Private, yes. In Hosted, we expose a smaller set of knobs: enable/disable caching per route, and some TTL/cap defaults. We’re careful because wrong settings can hurt p99.

[07:52] Karen Liu: That’s a big thing. We can’t accept latency regressions for our VIP customers.

[07:56] Omar El-Sayed: Understood. Actually caching usually improves p95 by reducing prefill compute, but it can add overhead if instrumentation or cache lookup is too heavy. We’ve been running perf-canary to enforce near-zero overhead.

[08:11] Allison Grant: And for alerts, we treat cache efficiency as a guardrail, not a pager for every dip. We do alert logic that tries to avoid workload mix false positives.

[08:23] Priya Desai: Like diurnal patterns.

[08:25] Allison Grant: Exactly. We look at hit-rate within prompt-length buckets and compare to a trailing baseline. If traffic shifts to shorter prompts, overall hit-rate will drop, but the bucketed hit-rate should be stable.

[08:40] Devon Marshall: That’s good. So you have histograms by prompt token count?

[08:44] Allison Grant: Buckets, yes. Not per exact token. Something like 0-256, 256-512, 512-1k, 1k-2k, 2k-4k, 4k+.

[08:56] Karen Liu: Can you show us the dashboard layout? Or at least describe it.

[09:01] Allison Grant: Sure. Top row is overall prefix cache hit-rate and KV reuse effectiveness trend, with filters for model, route, deployment mode, region. Next is miss reason breakdown stacked area (capacity vs TTL vs hash mismatch etc). Then eviction pressure and eviction rate. Then wasted prefill as tokens/sec and as % of prefill. And then comparisons: region A vs region B, or model version A vs B.

[09:30] Devon Marshall: That last one is key because we run US-East and EU-West.

[09:35] Omar El-Sayed: Region is also where routing locality comes in. If you’re routing a given conversation across regions, you’ll get near-zero reuse.

[09:44] Priya Desai: We try to keep sessions sticky, but during incidents we fail over.

[09:49] Omar El-Sayed: Yep. So our suggestion is policy-based routing: primary region for stickiness, fallback region only on capacity issues. Telemetry will show “locality breaks” indirectly as version/region mismatch misses and a drop in reuse depth.

[10:08] Karen Liu: Is there a direct metric for “routed to different cache pool”? Like a locality miss?

[10:13] Omar El-Sayed: We have an internal counter for “pool mismatch” but we don’t always expose it as a metric label because it can get cardinal. We can expose it as a miss reason category in the aggregate view, and in traces we can annotate when a request didn’t land on the expected locality.

[10:34] Devon Marshall: Traces meaning OpenTelemetry spans?

[10:36] Allison Grant: Yes, with annotations like “prefix_cache=hit, reused_tokens=2048” or “miss_reason=version_mismatch.” But sampled.

[10:49] Karen Liu: Okay. Another thing: streaming chat. We do server-sent events. We’ve seen weirdness where retries happen and metrics double count.

[10:59] Omar El-Sayed: Good catch. We had that bug internally—stream retries causing double counting. It’s fixed now. Telemetry treats a retried stream carefully: prefill is only counted once, and hits/misses are attributed to the final attempt. There’s still a nuance if the client reconnects mid-stream, but we bias toward not inflating hit-rate.

[11:25] Priya Desai: So can we rely on hit-rate not being “fake high” when retries occur?

[11:29] Omar El-Sayed: Yes. And we can add a “retry_count” field in traces, not metrics.

[11:37] Devon Marshall: Our biggest cost is prefill. Like 70% of tokens are prompt, not completion.

[11:43] Omar El-Sayed: That’s common in agentic systems. Prefix caching is the lever. If you can get, say, 40-60% reused prefill tokens for those long system prompts, your $/request can drop materially. Exact depends on batch size and model.

[12:02] Karen Liu: Can you quantify? Like if we have 3k system prompt, 500 user, 300 completion, average.

[12:09] Omar El-Sayed: Roughly: if system prompt is stable and you reuse 2.5k of it, you’re skipping that compute. You still pay for the tokens logically in some pricing models, but in our Dedicated pricing it translates into throughput. In Hosted, it can translate into lower per-token effective cost on our side, and we can pass some of that via pricing tiers—Miguel can speak more.

[12:29] Miguel Santos: Yeah, for Dedicated it’s straightforward: more requests per GPU-hour. For Hosted, pricing is usage-based but we use cache efficiency to keep our prices competitive. For an enterprise contract, we can structure it with committed spend plus performance expectations.

[12:48] Ben Torres: That’s what I care about. If we commit, we need predictability.

[12:52] Miguel Santos: Understood.

[12:55] Karen Liu: Back to telemetry. How do we join these metrics to our app events? We need per route at least, and we need to know model version.

[13:03] Allison Grant: We attach consistent join keys: route_id, model_id/model_version, deployment_mode, region. We don’t include raw prompt. For your side, you can propagate a request_id; we keep it in traces, not metrics.

[13:18] Priya Desai: So we can look at an outlier request in our logs and then find the trace.

[13:22] Allison Grant: Yes, assuming sampling includes it. For debugging incidents we can temporarily increase sampling on a route.

[13:32] Devon Marshall: Is there a way to detect telemetry gaps? Like if dashboards show zero hits because ingestion dropped labels.

[13:39] Allison Grant: We have drop detection. We alert on metric ingestion anomalies: sudden series count drop, or hit-rate goes to zero while request volume is steady. It’s a separate “telemetry pipeline health” dashboard.

[13:57] Karen Liu: Good. We had a vendor where the dashboard showed 0 for a week and no one noticed.

[14:05] Miguel Santos: Not great. Yeah, we treat that as a Sev-2 internally because it blocks optimization.

[14:12] Priya Desai: About labels… you said no tenant_id. Our routes are per product, not per tenant.

[14:18] Miguel Santos: That’s common. We can work with you on route strategy—like adding a small set of route variants for your top tenants, or a header-based “tenant cohort” tag that is an allowlist.

[14:33] Allison Grant: Exactly, we can allow a “tenant_tier” label with values like enterprise / smb / free. That’s manageable cardinality.

[14:42] Devon Marshall: That’s workable.

[14:45] Karen Liu: Okay, deployment. We’re leaning Dedicated because we need predictable throughput and some isolation. But we’re not doing on-prem.

[14:55] Miguel Santos: Dedicated makes sense. Then you can also opt into more granular telemetry because it’s your instance. We still enforce some sanity to avoid blowing up Prometheus, but it’s less constrained.

[15:10] Priya Desai: How does routing locality work in Dedicated? Is it a single pool?

[15:14] Omar El-Sayed: You can have multiple pools by region or by model. Locality is basically: keep a route pinned to a pool, and keep a conversation sticky to the same pool. If you do autoscaling with multiple replicas, we try to keep cache warm by consistent hashing of session keys.

[15:34] Devon Marshall: Consistent hashing on what? Conversation ID?

[15:37] Omar El-Sayed: Exactly. Or a cache key derived from the prefix hash. But you generally provide a session id header.

[15:48] Karen Liu: And if a node dies.

[15:50] Omar El-Sayed: Then you lose that node’s cache, hit-rate dips temporarily. Telemetry should show eviction/pressure doesn’t spike; instead you see capacity events and a sudden drop with recovery.

[16:06] Allison Grant: And that’s where alerts are nuanced. You don’t want a page every time a node rotates.

[16:12] Priya Desai: Right.

[16:14] Devon Marshall: One more question: Do you differentiate prefix cache and KV cache in naming? We’ve seen vendors mix them.

[16:21] Omar El-Sayed: We keep them distinct. Prefix cache metrics: reused_prefill_tokens, eligible_prefill_tokens, reuse_depth_histogram, prefix_cache_miss_reason. KV metrics: kv_reuse_tokens, kv_entries_active, kv_evictions, and “wasted_prefill_tokens” as a cross-signal.

[16:45] Karen Liu: Okay. What is “wasted prefill” exactly again?

[16:49] Omar El-Sayed: It’s prefill tokens computed that don’t end up enabling reuse later. Like you paid the compute cost but didn’t get amortization. It correlates strongly with thrash and poor locality. It’s not a moral judgment metric, it’s just highlighting inefficiency.

[17:10] Devon Marshall: Could it be high just because users churn and don’t come back?

[17:13] Omar El-Sayed: Yes. That’s why we always interpret it with traffic patterns. If conversations are one-and-done, caching across turns won’t help. Telemetry by route and prompt length helps identify where caching is expected.

[17:30] Karen Liu: Our usage is repeated. Support agents go back and forth.

[17:33] Devon Marshall: Also we have a lot of repeated tool schemas. Tools list is basically identical.

[17:38] Omar El-Sayed: Great. That’s the sweet spot.

[17:42] Ben Torres: I’m going to drop soon. Can you just tell me what we get in terms of reporting? Like weekly reports?

[17:49] Miguel Santos: For the pilot, we’ll provide weekly efficiency reports: hit-rate by key routes, cost per ticket proxy, and a list of recommended changes with expected impact. Longer term, it’s in Console / Optimize as a recommendations page.

[18:07] Ben Torres: Okay, thanks.

[18:10] Ben Torres: (drops)

[18:12] Karen Liu: So what do you need from us to estimate what hit-rate we can get?

[18:17] Omar El-Sayed: Two things: (1) prompt canonicalization feasibility—can you remove volatile fields from the cached prefix; (2) request shape distribution—prompt lengths, number of turns, and region distribution. If you can send a 24-hour histogram, we can model expected reuse.

[18:40] Devon Marshall: We can do that. But we can’t send raw prompts.

[18:43] Miguel Santos: We don’t need raw prompts. Just bucket counts.

[18:47] Priya Desai: What about data privacy overall? We’re SOC2, we need audit trails.

[18:52] Miguel Santos: Redwood is SOC 2, and we support audit logs, SSO, RBAC. On telemetry specifically, we don’t log raw prompts in metrics. Traces can include request IDs and some derived fields, but you control sampling and retention, especially on Dedicated.

[19:10] Allison Grant: And labels are allowlisted. If someone tries to attach a user_id label, ingestion drops it.

[19:17] Priya Desai: Good.

[19:20] Karen Liu: Let’s talk about false positives. If hit-rate dips, how do we know if it’s because our prompt changed or because cache is evicting.

[19:28] Allison Grant: That’s why miss reasons. Hash mismatch indicates prompt differences. Capacity/eviction indicates pressure. TTL expired indicates your TTL is too short or traffic spacing is too long. Version mismatch indicates rollouts.

[19:46] Omar El-Sayed: Also reuse depth. If depth collapses from 2k to 200 tokens, often the prefix template changed.

[19:56] Devon Marshall: Makes sense.

[20:00] Karen Liu: Do you have any gotchas we should know? Things that look like cache hits but aren’t.

[20:06] Omar El-Sayed: The big gotcha is continuous batching. When multiple requests are batched in prefill, naive instrumentation can misattribute reuse. We’ve corrected for that. Another gotcha is streaming retries. Also if you do tool calling where tool schema is serialized differently across calls, you’ll think it’s stable but it’s not.

[20:32] Devon Marshall: Yeah our JSON serializer is not stable across languages.

[20:35] Omar El-Sayed: That’s a common reason for hash mismatch. Recommendation can flag it.

[20:43] Priya Desai: On routing locality, if we have multi-region active-active, do we have to sacrifice that to get cache.

[20:50] Omar El-Sayed: You can do active-active but with session stickiness. Like users in EU stay EU. Don’t bounce a single conversation between EU and US. For failover, accept that hit-rate drops during the failover window.

[21:08] Karen Liu: Okay.

[21:10] Miguel Santos: We’re at around halfway. Anything else you want to cover?

[21:16] Devon Marshall: Could you share an example of a recommendation output? Like the text.

[21:20] Miguel Santos: Sure, rough example: “Route /support/chat: Prefix cache hit-rate 18% (down 22% WoW) driven by hash_mismatch misses in 2k-4k prompt bucket. Suggested actions: remove request_id and timestamp from system prefix; ensure tool list is sorted; enable prompt canonicalization. Expected impact: +20-35% reused prefill tokens; throughput +15%.” That kind of format.

[21:52] Karen Liu: That’s the right level.

[21:55] Allison Grant: We also include confidence and caveats. Like if traffic is too low, we’ll say low confidence.

[22:04] Priya Desai: Can we export telemetry to our own Datadog?

[22:08] Allison Grant: On Dedicated, yes—either scrape metrics endpoints or forward to your stack. On Hosted, you get it in Console plus export via APIs in some cases.

[22:21] Karen Liu: Great.

[22:23] Devon Marshall: I think we’re good. Can we recap next steps.

[22:27] Miguel Santos: Yep. Allison will send a panel list and screenshots, Omar will send metric definitions and sampling defaults. You’ll send a 24h request-shape summary and confirm deployment/regions. Then we schedule a follow-up next week to talk pilot plan and expected cache upside.

[22:51] Karen Liu: Works.

[22:53] Priya Desai: Thanks.

[22:55] Omar El-Sayed: Thanks all.

(Transcript ends — minor cross-talk and goodbye omitted)
